title: Bridge pattern
idea: The Bridge pattern splits one class hierarchy into two, an abstraction and an implementation, joined by a field, so each side can grow independently.

analogy.text: Camera bodies and lenses: any lens fits any body through one standard mount, so a new lens works with every body.
analogy.breaks: A mount is set by one maker; you design the implementor interface yourself.

points: Two dimensions in one hierarchy multiply classes: M reports times N formats.
The abstraction holds an implementor field and calls only its small primitive methods.
A new format or a new report is one class; neither side is edited.
JDBC is often cited as a bridge: one `Connection` API, many vendor drivers.

steps.caption: The abstraction side says WHAT a report contains. Subclasses add report logic, not formatting.
The implementor side says HOW to draw a header and a row. It knows nothing about invoices.
The bridge is one field: `Report` holds a `Renderer` passed in through its constructor.
The client picks one of each and joins them. Any report pairs with any renderer.
`StockReport.render()` decides the rows, then calls `out.row()`; the Markdown renderer draws them.
Adding an HTML format is one new `Renderer` class. Both reports gain it with no edits.

code.title: The problem: class grid
code.caption: Report type and output format welded into one hierarchy: one class per pair, and copies drift.

walk.text: Two reports times two formats is four classes. A third format makes six, a third report nine.
The CSV invoice quotes the item, because it contains a comma.
The CSV stock report was copied from it and lost the quoting: its row now has three columns.
The Markdown table syntax is repeated in every Markdown class.
Run it and compare the CSV rows: one format, two different rules.

code.title: The fix: a bridge
code.caption: Reports decide content, renderers decide format; a field joins them, so any pair works.

walk.text: The implementor interface is small and primitive: a header and a row. Keep it that way.
The abstraction holds the bridge as a `final` field and defensively copies its data.
`InvoiceReport` owns the total logic and never mentions commas or pipes.
`StockReport` owns the low-stock rule, again with no formatting code.
CSV quoting now lives in exactly one place, so every report gets it right.
The client composes pairs at runtime. M reports plus N formats is M + N classes.

pitfalls: An implementor with report-level methods like `renderInvoice` couples the sides again; keep its operations primitive.
Using Bridge for one dimension that varies adds an interface for nothing; wait for the second.
Calling it Strategy in an interview is incomplete: Bridge means both sides are hierarchies that vary.

quiz.q: A bridge has 3 report types and 4 formats. Adding a fifth format needs how many new classes?
quiz.why: Formats live only on the implementor side. One new `Renderer` class pairs with all three reports through the existing field.

takeaway: Bridge turns M times N subclasses into M plus N classes.

starters: How is the Bridge pattern different from the Strategy pattern?
